title: The Carbon Cycle: Nature's Balance
summary: How carbon moves between air, plants, animals, oceans, and soil in a natural, repeating cycle, why that balance matters, and how burning fossil fuels adds extra carbon to the air.
poll: What happens in the ocean and what happens in the forest are closely connected to each other.

versions.title: Carbon Goes Around
versions.text:
All living things have carbon in them. Carbon is in the air, too. It is part of a gas.

Plants take in that gas. They use the sun to make food. Plants keep carbon in their leaves.

Bugs and birds eat plants. Big ones eat small ones, too. This is how they get carbon. When they breathe out, they send some carbon back into the air.

When a plant dies, it breaks down. Some of its carbon goes into the soil.

Carbon moves from the air to plants. It moves on to bugs and birds, then to the soil. Then it goes back to the air. We call this a cycle. It happens again and again.

Folks burn coal and gas. This sends more carbon into the air. We must keep carbon in check to keep the Earth well.

versions.title: The Carbon Cycle: Nature's Balance
versions.text:
All living things have carbon in them. Carbon is also found in the air, as part of a gas called carbon dioxide. Carbon moves between air, plants, animals, oceans, and soil. This movement never stops.

Green plants take in carbon dioxide from the air. Through a process called photosynthesis, they use sunlight to turn it into food. Plants store carbon in their leaves, stems, and roots. This carbon stays there as the plant grows.

Animals get carbon by eating plants. Some animals eat other animals that ate plants. Through a process called respiration, animals release carbon dioxide back into the air when they breathe. This happens many times each day.

Oceans also absorb large amounts of carbon dioxide from the air. When a plant or animal dies, tiny bugs help it decompose. Its carbon becomes part of the soil, ready to be used again.

Carbon moves from the air into plants. It moves into animals, then into oceans and soil. Then it goes back into the air. This repeating path is the carbon cycle, and it has gone on for a very long time.

People burn coal, oil, and gas for power and travel. This sends extra carbon into the air faster than plants and oceans can absorb it. Keeping carbon in balance matters for a healthy climate and for every living thing on Earth.

versions.title: The Carbon Cycle: Nature's Balance
versions.text:
All living things are made partly of carbon. Carbon is also found in the air, as part of a gas known as carbon dioxide. Carbon is always circulating between the air, plants, animals, oceans, and soil in a pattern that scientists call the carbon cycle. This cycle has run for countless ages.

Green plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air. Through a biological process called photosynthesis, they use energy from sunlight to transform it into food. Plants store carbon within their leaves, stems, and roots as they grow and develop. This carbon can remain stored for a very long time.

Animals obtain carbon by consuming plants, or by consuming other animals that previously ate plants. Through a process called respiration, animals release carbon dioxide back into the air every time they breathe. This completes another part of the ongoing cycle, again and again, day after day.

Oceans also absorb truly enormous amounts of carbon dioxide from the air, holding much of it in their waters for long periods, sometimes many centuries. When a plant or an animal dies, bacteria help it decompose. Its carbon gradually becomes part of the soil, where growing plants can later take it up again.

Carbon travels continuously from the air, into plants, into animals, into oceans and soil, and back into the air once more. This endless journey has continued for millions of years.

People burn coal, oil, and gas for power, heat, and travel. This releases extra carbon into the air faster than plants and oceans alone can absorb it. Keeping this balance matters greatly for a healthy climate, both now and for many generations still to come.

versions.title: The Carbon Cycle: Nature's Balance
versions.text:
All living organisms are made partly of carbon, a fundamental element also found in the atmosphere as part of a gas known as carbon dioxide. Carbon circulates continuously between the atmosphere, plants, animals, oceans, and soil in a pattern that scientists call the carbon cycle, a system that has kept a rough equilibrium for millions of years. This balance long predates human beings.

Green plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Through a process called photosynthesis, they harness sunlight to transform it into food. Plants function as a temporary reservoir, storing carbon in their leaves, stems, and roots as they grow. This carbon remains stored until the plant eventually dies.

Animals obtain carbon by consuming plants, or by consuming other animals that fed on plants. Through a process called respiration, animals release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere every time they breathe. This small exchange happens constantly, all around the world, every day.

Oceans likewise absorb enormous quantities of carbon dioxide. Tiny floating organisms called phytoplankton, much like land plants, use sunlight to convert carbon into food, forming the base of the ocean's food web. Oceans and the rock beneath them act as vast reservoirs, holding carbon for exceptionally long periods, sometimes millions of years.

When a plant or animal dies, bacteria help it decompose, returning much of its carbon to the soil. Some carbon becomes buried and compressed over immense spans of time, eventually forming fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and gas.

Human combustion of these fossil fuels for power, heat, and travel releases large emissions of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, adding carbon faster than plants and oceans alone can absorb it. Maintaining the natural equilibrium of the carbon cycle matters greatly, since it helps regulate Earth's climate and sustains all living things on Earth.

versions.title: The Carbon Cycle: Nature's Balance
versions.text:
All living organisms are made partly of carbon, a fundamental element also found in the atmosphere as part of a gas known as carbon dioxide. Carbon circulates continuously and ceaselessly between the atmosphere, plants, animals, oceans, and soil in a pattern that scientists call the carbon cycle, a remarkably stable system that has kept a rough equilibrium for millions of years, long before human beings ever existed, and this balance has proven remarkably durable over time.

Green plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Through a process called photosynthesis, they harness sunlight to transform it into food and into the very tissues that make up their bodies. Plants function as a temporary reservoir, storing carbon in their leaves, stems, and roots as they grow, develop, and eventually die and decay, and this stored carbon then gradually returns to the wider world around it, completing one more link in the chain.

Animals obtain carbon by consuming plants, or by consuming other animals that fed on plants. Through a process called respiration, animals release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere every single time they breathe, completing another segment of this interconnected cycle that links every living creature on the planet, and this exchange happens constantly, all around the world, every single day, without ever truly pausing.

Oceans likewise absorb truly enormous quantities of carbon dioxide. Tiny floating organisms called phytoplankton, much like land plants, use sunlight to convert carbon into food, forming the base of the ocean's entire food web and sustaining countless other species. Oceans and the rock beneath them act as vast reservoirs, holding carbon for exceptionally long periods, sometimes millions of years at a stretch.

When a plant or animal dies, bacteria help it decompose, returning much of its carbon to the soil in an endless cycle of renewal. Some carbon becomes buried and compressed over immense spans of geological time, eventually forming fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas deep underground.

Human combustion of these fossil fuels for power, heat, and travel releases large emissions of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, adding carbon considerably faster than plants and oceans alone can absorb it. Maintaining the natural equilibrium of the carbon cycle matters greatly, since it helps regulate Earth's climate and sustains all living things, both now and for many generations to come.

versions.title: The Carbon Cycle: Nature's Balance
versions.text:
All living organisms are composed in part of a fundamental chemical element called carbon, which is also found abundantly in the atmosphere as part of a gas known as carbon dioxide; carbon circulates continuously and ceaselessly between the atmosphere, plants, animals, oceans, and soil in a natural, self-sustaining pattern that scientists refer to as the carbon cycle, a remarkably stable system that has maintained a delicate equilibrium for literally millions of years, long before human beings ever existed on this planet.

Green plants absorb carbon dioxide directly from the surrounding atmosphere, and through a remarkable biological process called photosynthesis, they skillfully harness energy from sunlight to transform that carbon dioxide into food and into the very living tissues that make up their bodies. In this important way, plants effectively function as a temporary reservoir, storing carbon within their leaves, stems, and roots as they steadily grow, develop, and eventually die and slowly decay.

Animals, for their part, obtain carbon by consuming plants directly, or by consuming other animals that previously fed upon plants; through an essential process called respiration, animals release carbon dioxide back into the surrounding atmosphere every single time they breathe, thereby completing yet another vital segment of this ongoing, deeply interconnected cycle that quietly links every living creature on the entire planet.

Oceans likewise absorb truly enormous quantities of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, and countless tiny floating organisms called phytoplankton, much like land plants, use sunlight to convert some of that carbon into food, forming the very base of the ocean's entire food web and sustaining an astonishing number of other species. Oceans, together with the rock and sediment lying beneath them, act as vast natural reservoirs, holding carbon securely for exceptionally long periods, sometimes for millions of years at a single stretch.

When a plant or an animal eventually dies, bacteria patiently help its remains decompose, gradually returning much of its carbon to the soil, where growing plants can later absorb it once again in an endless, repeating cycle of renewal. Some carbon, however, becomes buried and compressed over truly immense spans of geological time, eventually forming fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas deep underground.

Human combustion of these fossil fuels for power, heat, and transportation steadily releases substantial emissions of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, adding extra carbon considerably faster than plants and oceans alone are genuinely able to absorb it. Maintaining the delicate natural equilibrium of the carbon cycle matters enormously, because it helps regulate Earth's entire climate system and sustains all living things, both now and for countless generations still to come.

versions.title: The Carbon Cycle: Nature's Balance
versions.text:
All living organisms, without exception, are composed in part of a fundamental chemical element called carbon, which is also found abundantly throughout the atmosphere as part of a gas widely known as carbon dioxide; carbon circulates continuously and ceaselessly between the atmosphere, plants, animals, oceans, and soil in a natural, remarkably self-sustaining pattern that scientists universally refer to as the carbon cycle, an extraordinarily stable system that has maintained a delicate equilibrium for literally millions upon millions of years, long before human beings ever existed on this planet at all.

Green plants absorb carbon dioxide directly from the surrounding atmosphere, and through a truly remarkable biological process called photosynthesis, they skillfully and efficiently harness energy from sunlight to transform that carbon dioxide into usable food and into the very living tissues that make up their bodies entirely. In this genuinely important way, plants effectively function as a temporary reservoir, storing carbon securely within their leaves, stems, and roots as they steadily grow, develop, and eventually die and slowly decay back into the earth.

Animals, for their part, obtain carbon by consuming plants directly, or alternatively by consuming other animals that previously fed upon plants themselves; through an essential biological process called respiration, animals release carbon dioxide back into the surrounding atmosphere every single time they breathe, thereby completing yet another vital segment of this ongoing, deeply interconnected cycle that quietly and continuously links every living creature found on the entire planet.

Oceans likewise absorb truly enormous quantities of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, and countless tiny floating organisms called phytoplankton, much like land plants do, use sunlight to convert some of that carbon into usable food, forming the very foundational base of the ocean's entire food web and sustaining an astonishing number of other marine species as a result. Oceans, together with the rock and sediment lying far beneath them, act collectively as vast natural reservoirs, holding carbon securely for exceptionally long periods of time, sometimes for millions of years at a single uninterrupted stretch.

When a plant or an animal eventually dies, bacteria patiently and steadily help its remains decompose, gradually returning much of its stored carbon to the soil, where growing plants can later absorb it once again in an endless, continuously repeating cycle of renewal. Some carbon, however, becomes buried and compressed over truly immense spans of geological time, eventually forming valuable fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas deep underground, far from the surface.

Human combustion of these fossil fuels for power, heat, and transportation steadily and continuously releases substantial emissions of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, adding considerable extra carbon noticeably faster than plants and oceans alone are genuinely able to absorb it. Maintaining the delicate natural equilibrium of the carbon cycle matters enormously and profoundly, because it helps regulate Earth's entire climate system and sustains all living things everywhere, both now and for countless generations still yet to come.

keyWords.example: Under a microscope, the scientist could see thousands of phytoplankton in a single drop of seawater.

keyWords.definition: the process of burning something, which releases energy and gases
keyWords.example: The combustion of wood in the fireplace kept the cabin warm all night.

keyWords.definition: something, such as a gas, that is sent or given off into the air
keyWords.example: The factory installed new filters to lower its emission of harmful gases.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Phytoplankton are said to be the only users of carbon, and all other living things avoid it completely, even in the sea
Fossil fuels are said to form within a few years, so they will last a long time
Carbon circulates in a long-stable cycle, though human combustion now adds carbon faster than it can be absorbed
Oceans are said to release more carbon than they absorb, which is why the air is getting warmer
questions.why: The article shows carbon moving in a long-stable cycle, and explains that human combustion of fossil fuels now adds carbon faster than the cycle can absorb it.

wrong.A: Phytoplankton are one part of the cycle, but not the only organisms that use carbon.
wrong.B: In the article, fossil fuels form over immense spans of geological time, not a few years.
wrong.D: The article says oceans absorb enormous quantities of carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: According to the article, what role do phytoplankton play?
options: They burn fossil fuels for their energy, like tiny engines
They decompose dead animals on land, like tiny cleaners
They store carbon only within deep rock, like tiny stones
They turn sunlight into food, like tiny plants
questions.why: The article says phytoplankton use sunlight to convert carbon into food, forming the base of the ocean's food web.

wrong.A: Burning fossil fuels is a human activity, not something phytoplankton do.
wrong.B: Decomposing dead animals on land is done by bacteria, not phytoplankton.
wrong.C: Phytoplankton float in water; they do not store carbon only in deep rock.

questions.stem: According to the article, how do fossil fuels form?
options: Plants release them right after photosynthesis in the morning
Carbon is buried and compressed over vast spans of time
Oceans are said to manufacture them from salt and sunlight
Animals produce them through respiration alone, in their lungs
questions.why: In the article, some carbon becomes buried and compressed over immense spans of geological time, eventually forming fossil fuels.

wrong.A: Photosynthesis makes food, not fossil fuels, and not instantly.
wrong.C: Oceans are not described as manufacturing fossil fuels from salt water.
wrong.D: Respiration releases carbon dioxide; it does not produce fossil fuels.

questions.stem: What is the effect of human combustion of fossil fuels on the carbon cycle?
options: It is said to have no effect on the atmosphere
It removes carbon permanently from the whole cycle
It releases emissions faster than nature can absorb
It is said to cause phytoplankton to stop growing
questions.why: In the article, human combustion of fossil fuels releases substantial emissions of carbon dioxide faster than plants and oceans can absorb it.

wrong.A: The article says combustion adds carbon to the atmosphere.
wrong.B: The released carbon re-enters the cycle; it is not permanently removed.
wrong.D: Phytoplankton growth is not described as stopping.

questions.stem: In the article, the word reservoir most nearly means —
options: a type of small underwater animal
a short, sudden burst of released energy in the sky
a sudden release of gas into the air
a place where something is stored a long time
questions.why: The article describes oceans and buried rock as reservoirs, meaning places that hold carbon for long periods of time.

wrong.A: An animal is not what reservoir means.
wrong.B: A burst of energy is not what reservoir means.
wrong.C: A sudden gas release is closer to an emission, not a reservoir.

questions.stem: Why does the article describe the carbon cycle as having maintained 'equilibrium' before human activity increased emissions?
options: To claim that carbon never moved before humans existed
To show that carbon moving in and out had stayed balanced
To suggest that oceans used to be frozen
To explain why plants once lacked the ability to grow
questions.why: Equilibrium describes a long-standing balance, showing that carbon moving in and out of the cycle stayed roughly steady for millions of years.

wrong.A: In the article, carbon has always circulated through the cycle.
wrong.C: Frozen oceans are not discussed.
wrong.D: The article does not say plants once could not grow.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might scientists pay close attention to carbon emissions today?
options: Because emissions add carbon faster than the cycle can balance
Because emissions make soil infertile in days
Because emissions stop all plants from photosynthesizing in the world
Because emissions are the main source of carbon on Earth
questions.why: The article explains that combustion releases carbon faster than plants and oceans can absorb it, upsetting the cycle's natural equilibrium.

wrong.B: Soil fertility within days is not discussed.
wrong.C: Photosynthesis stopping entirely is not discussed.
wrong.D: The article describes many natural sources of carbon, not just emissions.

questions.stem: How does the role of plants compare with the role of oceans in the carbon cycle, according to the article?
options: Both plants and phytoplankton use sunlight to make food
Plants only release carbon, while oceans only absorb it
Oceans use carbon for breathing, like animals
Plants and oceans play no related role in the cycle
questions.why: The article says phytoplankton, much like land plants, use sunlight to convert carbon into food, showing a similar role for plants and ocean organisms.

wrong.B: Plants absorb carbon through photosynthesis; they do not only release it.
wrong.C: Oceans are described as absorbing carbon, not using it only for breathing.
wrong.D: The article shows plants and oceans both play important, related roles.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why burning fossil fuels affects the natural equilibrium of the carbon cycle. Use the words combustion and emission, and support your explanation with evidence.
checklist: I explained how fossil fuels form.
I explained the effect of burning them.
I used combustion and emission correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Fossil fuels form when carbon from dead plants and animals becomes buried and compressed over immense spans of geological time, acting as a long-term reservoir of carbon. When people use combustion to burn these fossil fuels for power, heat, and transportation, they release emissions of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere much faster than plants and oceans can absorb it. Because the natural carbon cycle took millions of years to reach a stable equilibrium, adding carbon this quickly through combustion disturbs that balance.

options: In their leaves
In their seeds
In the air
In the sun
LOW.why: The text says plants keep carbon in their leaves.

wrong.B: Seeds are not mentioned in the text.
wrong.C: Carbon is in the air, but plants take it in and keep it in leaves.
wrong.D: The sun gives plants power to make food, but they do not keep carbon in it.

LOW.stem: How do bugs and birds get carbon?
options: They drink the rain.
They eat plants.
They sit in the sun.
They dig in the soil.
LOW.why: In the text, bugs and birds eat plants, and this is how they get carbon.

wrong.A: Rain is not mentioned as a way to get carbon.
wrong.C: Sunlight helps plants make food, not bugs and birds.
wrong.D: Digging in soil is not how they get carbon in the text.

LOW.stem: Which list shows the path of carbon in the article?
options: Soil, bugs and birds, air, plants
Plants, air, soil, bugs and birds
Air, plants, bugs and birds, soil
Bugs and birds, soil, plants, air
LOW.why: In the text, carbon moves from the air to plants, then to bugs and birds, then to the soil, then back to the air.

wrong.A: Carbon does not start in the soil in the text.
wrong.B: Carbon goes from the air to plants, not from plants to air first.
wrong.D: Carbon does not start with bugs in the text.

LOW.stem: What would most likely happen if folks burned less coal and gas?
options: Plants would stop growing in soil.
Birds would need to breathe less.
The soil would get a lot hotter.
Less carbon would go into the air.
LOW.why: In the text, burning coal and gas sends more carbon into the air, so burning less would send less.

wrong.A: The text does not say burning less would stop plants.
wrong.B: Birds' breathing is not linked to burning in the text.
wrong.C: The text does not link burning to hotter soil.

MID.stem: According to the article, where do plants store carbon?
options: In the oceans, rocks, and soil
In the air, clouds, and rain
In their leaves, stems, and roots
In their flowers, seeds, and fruit
MID.why: The text says plants store carbon in their leaves, stems, and roots.

wrong.A: Oceans and soil take in carbon, but plants do not store it there.
wrong.B: Carbon in the air is what plants take in.
wrong.D: Flowers and fruit are not mentioned in the text.

MID.stem: In the article, the word decompose means —
options: to grow tall
to break down
to float away
to make food
MID.why: In the text, bugs help a dead plant or animal decompose, and its carbon becomes part of the soil, so it breaks down.

wrong.A: Dead plants do not grow tall.
wrong.C: The carbon goes into the soil, not away.
wrong.D: Making food is what living plants do.

MID.stem: Which path matches the carbon cycle in the article?
options: Soil, oceans, air, plants, animals
Air, animals, plants, oceans, soil
Plants, soil, air, animals, oceans
Air, plants, animals, oceans, soil
MID.why: The text says carbon moves from the air into plants, then animals, then oceans and soil, and then back into the air.

wrong.A: Carbon does not start in the soil in the text.
wrong.B: Carbon goes into plants before animals.
wrong.C: Carbon goes from the air into plants first.

MID.stem: What would best help keep the carbon cycle in balance?
options: Burning less coal, oil, and gas
Cutting down more plants
Making more cars and power
Using more power for travel
MID.why: The text says burning coal, oil, and gas adds extra carbon too fast, so burning less would help balance.

wrong.B: Plants take in carbon, so fewer plants would not help.
wrong.C: More power and cars would add more carbon.
wrong.D: Travel uses fuels that add carbon to the air.

HIGH.stem: According to the article, how long can oceans and rock hold carbon?
options: Only for a few short days
For exactly one single year
Until the next rainy season
Sometimes millions of years
HIGH.why: The text says oceans and the rock beneath them hold carbon for exceptionally long periods, sometimes millions of years.

wrong.A: A few days is far too short for a reservoir.
wrong.B: The text gives no exact one-year time.
wrong.C: The text says very long periods, not one season.

HIGH.stem: In the article, the word fundamental most nearly means —
options: basic and necessary
rare and costly
new and unknown
small and light
HIGH.why: Carbon is part of all living organisms, so it is a basic and necessary element.

wrong.B: Carbon is common in living things, not rare.
wrong.C: The text says carbon has been in the cycle for millions of years.
wrong.D: The text does not describe carbon by its size or weight.

HIGH.stem: What happens to carbon when bacteria help a dead plant or animal decompose?
options: Most of it is burned as fuel.
Much of it returns to the soil.
All of it floats into space.
It turns into new phytoplankton.
HIGH.why: The text says bacteria help a dead organism decompose, returning much of its carbon to the soil.

wrong.A: Fuels form from buried carbon over long ages, not from bacteria acting at once.
wrong.C: Space is not mentioned in the text.
wrong.D: Phytoplankton use carbon in the ocean; they are not made by bacteria.

HIGH.stem: According to the article, what do scientists call the pattern in which carbon moves between the air, living things, oceans, and soil?
options: the water cycle
the carbon cycle
the food chain
the greenhouse
HIGH.why: The article says carbon circulates in a pattern scientists call the carbon cycle.

wrong.A: The water cycle moves water, not carbon.
wrong.C: A food chain is not the name given.
wrong.D: The greenhouse effect is about trapped heat, not this pattern.
